replacements.old_heading: Two People Are Enough to Fill a Screen
replacements.old_body: On November 29, 1972, the Computer History Museum dates Atari's announcement of Pong. The date should not be confused with earlier prototype tests in California bars, nor with the home versions that would arrive years later. Pong began as the first project assigned to Allan Alcorn at the young Atari founded by Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney. On screen are two paddles, a ball and a score: almost nothing, and for that very reason every element must be immediately understandable. The game turns a television into a social space in which two people read trajectories, anticipate rebounds and learn through a few seconds of practice. The commercial success of that simplicity helps Atari grow and makes Pong one of the symbols of the emerging coin-operated video game industry.
replacements.heading: An Atari arcade game
replacements.body: Pong is a 1972 sports video game developed and published by Atari, Inc. for arcades. It was created by Allan Alcorn as a training exercise assigned to him by Atari co-founder Nolan Bushnell. Bushnell and Atari co-founder Ted Dabney were so surprised by the quality of Alcorn's work that they decided to manufacture the game. Bushnell based the game's concept on an electronic ping-pong game included on the Magnavox Odyssey, the first home video game console; in response, Magnavox later sued Atari for patent infringement.

replacements.old_heading: The Date Marks an Announcement, Not an Instantaneous Invention
replacements.old_body: November 29, 1972 is useful precisely because it forces a distinction among the stages of Pong's history. The Computer History Museum records Atari's announcement of the game on this date, while the prototype designed by Allan Alcorn had already been built and tested. An accurate calendar should not turn every anniversary into an implausible day zero. Pong emerged through design, field testing, public response and later commercialization. The announcement belongs to that process and marks the moment when Atari formally presents a product destined to become central to the young company. Separating prototype from announcement makes the history more interesting, because it shows that success does not come from a single isolated intuition: it depends on how a simple technical solution is tested, recognized and turned into industrial activity.
replacements.heading: Two paddles and eleven points
replacements.body: Pong is a two-dimensional sports game that simulates table tennis. The player controls an in-game paddle by moving it vertically across the left or right side of the screen. They can compete against another player controlling a second paddle on the opposing side. Players use the paddles to hit a ball back and forth. The goal is for each player to reach eleven points before the opponent; points are earned when one fails to return the ball to the other.

replacements.old_heading: PAC-MAN Makes a Maze Readable and Invents a Global Language
replacements.old_body: On May 22, 1980 Namco held the first focus test of Puck Man, the game that would become PAC-MAN. The official site specifies that public release in Japan began in July, so this date marks the first test rather than a false worldwide launch. From that maze emerged one of the medium's most recognizable characters. PAC-MAN's strength lies in clarity: eat dots, avoid ghosts, use power pellets and read patterns. A few rules become space for strategy, character and popular culture.
replacements.heading: A maze chase from Namco
replacements.body: Pac-Man, originally titled Puck Man in Japan, is a 1980 maze video game developed and published by Namco for arcades. It was released in Japan on May 22, 1980 and by Midway Manufacturing in North America in October 1980. The player controls Pac-Man, who must eat all the dots inside an enclosed maze while avoiding four colored ghosts. Eating large flashing dots called "Power Pellets" causes the ghosts to temporarily turn blue and vulnerable, allowing Pac-Man to eat the ghosts for bonus points.

replacements.old_heading: A Game Designed Beyond Space War
replacements.old_body: Toru Iwatani sought an idea different from the shooters and war themes common in arcades. Food offered a more everyday vocabulary and made it possible to imagine a broader audience. The central action, eating, is immediately readable even before scores or strategies are understood. This thematic choice does not make PAC-MAN shallow. Instead, it creates a friendly frame within which an increasingly demanding system can exist. Accessibility comes from the metaphor, while depth emerges from movement through the maze. The consequence extends beyond one feature. PAC-MAN uses Toru Iwatani, audience and food theme to turn a concrete choice into rhythm, memory and behavior, making the system a recognizable part of the work's identity.
replacements.heading: Toru Iwatani and a broader audience
replacements.body: Pac-Man was designed by Toru Iwatani, who led a nine-man team; the game's development began in early 1979. Iwatani wanted to create a game that could appeal to women as well as men, because most video games of the time had themes that appealed to traditionally masculine interests, such as war or sports. Although the inspiration for the Pac-Man character was the image of a pizza with a slice removed, Iwatani has said he rounded out the Japanese character for mouth, kuchi (Japanese: 口). The in-game characters were made to be cute and colorful to appeal to younger players. The original Japanese title of Puck Man was derived from the Japanese phrase paku paku taberu, which refers to gobbling something up; the title was changed to Pac-Man for the North American release due to fears of vandals defacing cabinets by converting the P into an F, as in fuck.

replacements.old_heading: The Maze Is Small but Not Neutral
replacements.old_body: PAC-MAN's map fits on one screen, yet its routes are not equivalent. Side tunnels, intersections, corners and riskier zones determine opportunities for escape and pursuit. Players learn to read the space almost like a score, anticipating where ghosts may converge. A dynamic camera is unnecessary because all essential information is already present. Difficulty comes from interpreting it in real time. The maze is compact but structured enough to support learning and memory across hundreds of plays. This is where a design detail becomes language. In PAC-MAN, maze layout and routes guides attention and expectation, so technique stops being invisible and begins producing meaning through play.
replacements.heading: Eating every dot in the maze
replacements.body: Pac-Man is an action maze chase video game; the player controls the eponymous character through an enclosed maze. The objective of the game is to eat all of the dots placed in the maze while avoiding four colored ghosts—Blinky (red), Pinky (pink), Inky (cyan), and Clyde (orange)—who pursue Pac-Man. When Pac-Man eats all of the dots, the player advances to the next level. Levels are indicated by fruit icons at the bottom of the screen. In between levels are short cutscenes featuring Pac-Man and Blinky in humorous, comical situations.

replacements.old_body: Blinky, Pinky, Inky and Clyde are not simply four colored copies of the same enemy. Their behaviors create different pressures and make pursuit less predictable. Even without knowing exact formulas, players can feel that the ghosts distribute themselves through space with distinct personalities. Character therefore emerges from an algorithm rather than dialogue. This is one of PAC-MAN's most durable insights: an opponent can be memorable because its behavior produces a recognizable relationship with the player. This passage explains why PAC-MAN remains interesting beyond its date. ghosts, behaviors and reading is not isolated, but a node connecting production, rules and player perception inside the same experience.
replacements.heading: Four ghosts with different strategies
replacements.body: If Pac-Man is caught by a ghost, he loses a life; the game ends when all lives are lost. Each of the four ghosts has its own unique artificial intelligence (A.I.), or "personality": Blinky gives direct chase to Pac-Man; Pinky and Inky try to position themselves in front of Pac-Man, usually by cornering him; and Clyde switches between chasing and fleeing from Pac-Man depending on his distance from him.
